amt-amc-practice-1-upr-01.title: Spending minus takings
amt-amc-practice-1-upr-01.body:
Total spent: $34+14=48$ dollars. Money taken: $29$ dollars. Loss: $48-29=19$ dollars.

**Answer: (C) \$19**

amt-amc-practice-1-upr-01.title: Subtract each cost in turn
amt-amc-practice-1-upr-01.body:
After paying for lemons, the takings of \$29 leave $29-34=-5$, i.e. \$5 short. Paying \$14 for sugar as well makes it $5+14=19$ dollars short.

**Answer: (C) \$19**

amt-amc-practice-1-upr-02.title: Add up the outside edges
amt-amc-practice-1-upr-02.body:
The overlap square has area $16$ cm², so its side is $4$ cm. Each big square has two full sides of $10$ cm on the outside, and its other two sides are cut by the overlap into a $6$ cm part outside and a $4$ cm part inside.

Going round the combined shape: $4$ sides of $10$ cm and $4$ pieces of $10-4=6$ cm. Perimeter:
$$4\times10+4\times6=40+24=64\text{ cm}.$$

**Answer: (C) 64**

amt-amc-practice-1-upr-02.title: Subtract the hidden edges
amt-amc-practice-1-upr-02.body:
The two big squares have total perimeter $2\times40=80$ cm. The edges inside the combined shape are exactly the four sides of the overlap square, which has side $4$ cm and perimeter $16$ cm. So the outline is $80-16=64$ cm.

**Answer: (C) 64**

amt-amc-practice-1-upr-03.title: Work backwards
Simplify the steps
amt-amc-practice-1-upr-03.body:
Multiplying by $2$, adding $2$ and dividing by $2$ is the same as just adding $1$ (since $(2n+2)\div2=n+1$). Then subtracting $2$ gives $n+1-2=n-1$. So $n-1=2$ and $n=3$.

**Answer: (C) 3**

amt-amc-practice-1-upr-04.title: Try some possible scores
amt-amc-practice-1-upr-04.body:
Pick a few scores for Brian and work out the others (Sally $=2\times$ Brian, Corrie $=$ Sally $-30$, Donna $=$ Brian $+50$):

| Brian | Sally | Corrie | Donna |
|---|---|---|---|
| 15 | 30 | 0 | 65 |
| 50 | 100 | 70 | 100 |
| 55 | 110 | 80 | 105 |

* Row 1: Sally didn't win, Corrie (not Brian) came last, Corrie didn't beat Brian — so (A), (B), (D) can be false.
* Row 3: Sally beat Donna, so (C) can be false.
* (E): Sally is $30$ more than Corrie and Donna is $50$ more than Brian, so Sally $+$ Donna is always $80$ more than Brian $+$ Corrie. Always true.

**Answer: (E)**

amt-amc-practice-1-upr-04.title: Compare totals directly
amt-amc-practice-1-upr-04.body:
We don't need actual scores for (E): 
$$\text{Sally}+\text{Donna} = (\text{Corrie}+30)+(\text{Brian}+50) = \text{Brian}+\text{Corrie}+80,$$
which is always more than Brian $+$ Corrie. For the others, a single example (like Brian $15$, Sally $30$, Corrie $0$, Donna $65$, or Brian $55$, Sally $110$, Corrie $80$, Donna $105$) shows they can fail.

**Answer: (E)**

amt-amc-practice-1-upr-05.title: Make the others as small as possible
amt-amc-practice-1-upr-05.body:
To make the largest number as big as possible, make the other four as small as possible. Four different whole numbers are at least $1+2+3+4=10$, so the largest is at most $30-10=20$, and $1+2+3+4+20=30$ shows $20$ is possible.

**Answer: (D) 20**

amt-amc-practice-1-upr-05.title: Check the choices from the top
amt-amc-practice-1-upr-05.body:
* $26$: the other four would add up to $4$, but four different whole numbers add up to at least $10$. ✗
* $20$: the other four add up to $10$: $1,2,3,4$ ✓.

So the greatest possible value is $20$.

**Answer: (D) 20**

amt-amc-practice-1-upr-06.title: Blocks in one slice
amt-amc-practice-1-upr-06.body:
Look at the end of the staircase: it is a step shape with columns $8, 7, 6, \ldots, 1$ blocks high, so it has $8+7+\cdots+1=36$ blocks. Each block of width adds one such slice.

The cube has $12\times12\times12=1728$ blocks, so the width is
$$\frac{12\times12\times12}{36}=\frac{12\times12\times12}{12\times3} = 12\times4=48.$$

**Answer: 48**

amt-amc-practice-1-upr-06.title: Check with the small staircase
amt-amc-practice-1-upr-06.body:
The small staircase in the picture has end slices of $4+3+2+1=10$ blocks and is $5$ wide, so it uses $50$ blocks — the number of blocks is (blocks in one end slice) $\times$ (width).

For the big staircase, an end slice has $1+2+\cdots+8 = \frac{8\times9}{2}=36$ blocks. We need $36\times(\text{width}) = 1728$, so width $= 1728\div36 = 48$.

**Answer: 48**
